question: In the revision of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/361, the Commission intends to delete the reference to the Terrestrial Animal Health Code of the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) in Part 4 of Annex VII1 to the Regulation.

This would mean that, in the event of an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease (FMD), only emergency vaccination followed by the culling or slaughter of the vaccinated animals would be permitted in future. This would rule out the use of the ‘vaccinate to live’2 strategy, which has been possible until now.

The German Federal-State Working Group on Foot-and-Mouth Disease Vaccination Strategy, led by the German Federal Ministry of Food, Agriculture and Rural Affairs and involving the Robert Koch Institute and the Friedrich Loeffler Institute, has spoken out strongly against this planned deletion. 1.

How does the Commission justify the planned deletion of the reference to the WOAH Terrestrial Animal Health Code in Annex VII, Part 4 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/361, which has hitherto allowed the use of emergency vaccination without subsequent killing, even in the case of foot-and-mouth disease?

Did the Commission take into account the technical assessments and recommendations of the German Federal-State Working Group on Foot-and-Mouth Disease Vaccination Strategy when it decided to make the planned deletion?
In deciding on this deletion, did the Commission take into account the fact that a new vaccine against FMD is now available3, which has been proven to prevent infection in cloven-hoofed animals4?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.1.2026) Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/3611 (hereafter ‘the Regulation’), is in the process of being amended after extensive discussion in the relevant expert group.

The Regulation will continue to allow emergency vaccination against foot-and-mouth disease (FMD), either as suppressive vaccination or as protective vaccination, under the conditions defined in the Regulation.

The envisaged deletion of the reference to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) Terrestrial Animal Health Code2 will not remove the possibility to ‘vaccinate to live’, and it had never been a way to derogate from the requirements of the Regulation or provide for alternative recovery options.

Its deletion ensures that the applicable conditions derive directly from EU legislation, which must operate independently of external standards, that in addition have been modified since the Regulation was first adopted.

When emergency protective vaccination is applied for FMD, the Regulation already provides that movement restrictions in the vaccination zone remain in place for at least three months after the killing or slaughter of the last vaccinated animals. The use of vaccination, and the duration and territorial scope of the vaccination zone is decided by individual Member States.

The Commission takes into account scientific and technical input from Member States, including from the German authorities. The Commission also follows developments in FMD vaccines, including in new generation products.
